They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident presents a material safety risk, and provide periodic updates until the risk is resolved.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident presents a material safety risk, and provide periodic updates until the risk is resolved.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident presents a material safety risk, and provide periodic updates until the risk is resolved. Reports must include known circumstances, model and serial number, injuries or property damage, and corrective actions. A missed initial report must be disclosed promptly when discovered.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A model's failure rate must not exceed 8%. Any result above 8% requires prompt submission of a corrective-action plan to the regulator and retesting within 6 months; regulators may restrict sales if the model remains above 8%. Customers considering or purchasing a model must receive its numerical failure rate, test outcome, any applicable corrective-action plan, and any sales restriction.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and statistically adequate sample. Manufacturers must submit per-model numerical results and test methods confidentially to regulators. Customers considering or purchasing a model must receive its numerical failure rate, test outcome, any applicable corrective-action plan, and any sales restriction. A model’s failure rate must not exceed 8%. Any result above 8% requires prompt submission of a corrective-action plan to the regulator and retesting within 6 months; regulators may restrict sales if the model remains above 8%. Regulators may publish aggregate results, but not individual-company per-model failure rates.

parameters.quote: All new units must support remote emergency shut-off at the time of sale. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that do not support the function, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved safety measure, within 6 years after adoption.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new units must support remote emergency shut-off at the time of sale. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that do not support the function, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved safety measure, within 6 years after adoption.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new units must support remote emergency shut-off at the time of sale. Manufacturers must retrofit installed units that do not support the function, or provide an equivalent regulator-approved safety measure, within 6 years after adoption. Shut-off capability must be available to authorized emergency responders and customers, with safeguards against unauthorized activation.

parameters.quote: All new units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: All new units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be appropriate to the battery chemistry and enclosure, independently validated, and maintained in working order throughout the unit’s service life. Manufacturers must provide customers with instructions for inspection and any required maintenance.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A rate above 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year requires prompt regulator review and a public determination of whether recall or other protective action is necessary; it does not by itself automatically trigger a recall.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Customers must receive clear, model-specific safety notices promptly when a manufacturer or regulator identifies a material safety risk, including known hazards, affected units, immediate precautions, and available remedies; manufacturers must update notices as material information changes. Regulators may require corrective action, sales restrictions, or a recall based on incident rates, severity, trends, and other evidence. A rate above 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year requires prompt regulator review and a public determination of whether recall or other protective action is necessary; it does not by itself automatically trigger a recall.

judge_section_notes: S2 sets the permanent failure limit at 8%, not the 5% discussed, and any above-limit model may keep selling unless regulators choose to restrict it, which protects Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%). S5 makes a rate above 8/100k a review trigger rather than an automatic recall, protecting Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9/100k). S3's six-year retrofit (Northwind's red line) and S4's 36-month suppression start (Halcyon's red line) sit at the edges of their acceptable ranges, and S2 nonetheless gives customers numeric per-model rates (Halcyon's red line) while keeping them off the public record.
